doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Rap, the negative side of music, and vibration
summary: Jeannie and Jimmy discuss rap and cuts to school music, and Jimmy talks of sound as vibration.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: See I know they can. And I’m quite sure that the powers that be, that keep saying that we don’t need music in the schools —

That’s more negative than rap, and I like rap on certain things, because they have a lot of people that teach very interesting things through rap. And the rhythm of the words is a power in itself. It’s almost like haiku poetry if you want to talk about. Because that’s in a sense, an art form in itself. One day we’re going to probably peel away a couple of verses and things and say, oh this is really poetry, it’s wonderful poetry. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Another interesting thing, not to oversimplify, but to me it’s like getting right into the source, like looking into the sun but not too long because you can become blind as a bat. But the thing is is that we look at sound. Sound does not happen unless it has a vibrating body in some way, shape, form or fashion. But sound itself, the nature of sound, is emanated from a vibration. There is nothing that exists on this planet earth or in its environment or the universe that doesn’t have, is not affected by vibration. The sun rays. How many miles — they say how many million miles, 83 million or something like that? But nobody’s got that close to find out about it. But the point is, by even projecting that, you know that you feel the vibration of that heat. You follow me? And so that has to have, without a doubt, whatever, knowingly or unknowingly, some aspect of effect from a scientific point of view, on every living thing on this planet. Man.
We’ll have to sit and analyze that.
